uncited: It differs from backward ray-marching by allowing early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible, and it decouples the physical density data from visual appearance rules via material parameterization and gradient-based classification as defined in [Specific Material and Geometry Rendering](4395-specific-material-and-geometry-rendering.md).

- **Inputs:** Camera position, view direction per pixel, depth buffer (for scene intersection reconstruction), light position and intensity, fog density ($\tau$), scattering coefficient ($a$), and phase function parameters.
- **Depth Buffer:** 2D texture or array storing depth values $z$ for each pixel UV coordinate.
Define the ray origin as the camera position and the ray direction as the vector from the camera to the reconstructed intersection point.
**Ray Marching Loop:** Iterate from the camera (start) to the scene intersection (finish) at regular intervals $\Delta l$.
-   Calculate the current sample position $x(l_n)$ along the ray.
-   Calculate the distance $l_n$ traveled from the camera to the current sample.
-   Calculate the in-scattering term $L_i(x(l_n), \omega)$ for the current sample.
-   Update transmittance for the next step: $T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\tau \Delta l}$.
**Final Composition:** Combine the accumulated fog radiance with the background scene color (if applicable) using the final transmittance.
-   **Step Size ($\Delta l$):** Determines the resolution of the ray march.
Smaller steps reduce artifacts but increase computation.
-   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot S)$, where $N$ is the number of pixels and $S$ is the number of steps per ray.
-   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ per pixel, plus storage for depth buffer and light shadow maps if used.
-   **Performance:** Real-time performance is achievable with Schlick phase function approximation and early-out optimizations.
Step size significantly impacts performance and visual quality.
-   **When to Use:** Real-time fog effects in games or applications where dynamic lighting interaction is required.
-   **When Not to Use:** When high-fidelity, artifact-free volumetric rendering is required without post-processing, or when performance is extremely constrained.
